tours.title: How to Spend a Day in Atlanta's Sweet Auburn Historic District
Exploring Sweet Auburn: A Civil Rights History Tour
Martin Luther King, Jr. National Historical Park - Places To Go

stops.name: Auburn Avenue Research Library on African American Culture and History
stops.description: The first library in the Southeast built for archival research into African American history, holding more than 600 manuscript collections and a quarter-million photographs.

stops.name: APEX Museum
stops.description: Atlanta's oldest Black history museum, which tells the story of Sweet Auburn from the perspective of the people who built it.

stops.name: Atlanta Daily World Building
stops.description: From 1928 to 2008 this 1912 building published the Atlanta Daily World, the country's oldest continuously running Black daily newspaper, and it was restored after a 2008 tornado tore off its roof.

stops.name: The Royal Peacock
stops.description: The Auburn Avenue club where Little Richard, Aretha Franklin and James Brown played on the chitlin' circuit, still operating as a nightclub today.

stops.name: Big Bethel A.M.E. Church
stops.description: Atlanta's oldest Black congregation, founded in 1847, identifiable a block away by the lit JESUS SAVES sign on its steeple.

stops.name: Sweet Auburn Curb Market
stops.description: A public market since 1918 that moved into this building in 1924, now home to about thirty butchers, produce stalls and lunch counters.

stops.name: Madame C.J. Walker Museum and WERD Radio Studio
stops.description: WERD went on the air here in 1949 as the first Black-owned radio station in the country, in a building that also housed a Walker beauty shop.

stops.name: Wheat Street Baptist Church
stops.description: Rev. William Holmes Borders led this congregation for fifty years and ran the boycotts that desegregated Atlanta's buses and downtown stores.

stops.name: Historic Ebenezer Baptist Church
stops.description: Martin Luther King Jr. was baptized and later co-pastored in this sanctuary, restored by the Park Service in 2001 to how it looked in his day.

stops.name: The King Center
stops.description: Founded by Coretta Scott King in 1968, its reflecting pool holds the Georgia marble crypt of Dr. and Mrs. King beside an eternal flame.

stops.name: BEHOLD Monument
stops.description: A bronze sculpture of a father lifting his newborn skyward, drawn from an African naming ritual and inscribed with the closing lines of the Dream speech.

stops.name: I Have a Dream World Peace Rose Garden
stops.description: A starburst-shaped bed of 185 roses on Peace Plaza, ringed by messages of peace written by schoolchildren from Atlanta and around the world.

stops.name: Martin Luther King Jr. Birth Home
stops.description: King was born in this Queen Anne house in 1929 and lived here until he was twelve; it reopened on July 4, 2026 after nearly three years of restoration.

stops.name: Historic Fire Station No. 6
stops.description: An 1894 Romanesque Revival firehouse that became one of Atlanta's first integrated stations and now shows a restored 1927 pumper truck.

stops.name: Jackson Street Bridge
stops.description: An ordinary overpass with the best free view of the downtown skyline, looking west across Freedom Parkway and the Downtown Connector.

note: First run of this scout, so no city had a turn yet and Atlanta won alphabetically. Batch is deliberately one cluster: the Auburn Avenue corridor from 101 Auburn east to 501 Auburn is about 0.6 mi, plus a 0.4 mi spur north up Jackson St to the bridge overlook. Dropped the Martin Luther King Jr. NHP Visitor Center at 450 Auburn Ave: NPS says the visitor center is temporarily relocated to Fire Station No. 6, so the building itself is not currently visitable. Its outdoor Peace Plaza features, the rose garden and the BEHOLD monument, are still listed by NPS and kept. A fourth tour was read and held back rather than used: Downtown Atlanta Inc's self-guided Modern Renaissance walk (https://downtownatlantainc.com/post/self-guided-walking-tour-downtown-atlanta) covers Walton Spring Park, the American Hotel, Centennial Olympic Park, State Farm Arena and the stadium, but those sit 1.5 mi west of Sweet Auburn and would have split the cluster. They are a good basis for a separate downtown-core batch. Two other candidate sources returned HTTP 403 and could not be opened, so nothing was taken from them: theclio.com/tour/107 and the Discover Atlanta Auburn Avenue itinerary. Wheat Street Baptist Church is filed at its sanctuary address, 359 Auburn Ave NE, not the 18 William Holmes Borders Sr Dr office address that some listings show.
